notes: The whole 58-page PDF, read end to end: the introduction and methodology, Part 1 on the suburbanisation context, Part 2's history of the district from its natural history to its demographics, Part 3's property types and Notable Buildings, the Next Steps and Conclusion, every figure caption, every footnote and the bibliography. This is a narrative context statement with no appendix inventory table and no APNs anywhere; its address-level material is concentrated in one place — the three lists under “Other Structures of Interest” on p. 50 (Parkside Cottages, Other Residential, Commercial/Civic/Religious) — with the rest scattered through the six Notable Buildings write-ups, the photograph captions and the footnotes. Two things govern how it must be read. First, the report writes house numbers on the numbered avenues in the Western Neighborhoods Project's house style, hyphenated: “2476-20th Avenue” means 2476 20th Avenue, not a range, and a range-aware reader will mis-parse every one of them. Second, the report is scrupulous about pre-1909 street names — the Sunset and Parkside streets were lettered (T Street for Taraval, H Street for Lincoln Way) until the Parkside Realty Company petitioned for full names, and the statement uses the letter name when writing about pre-1909 events — so no lettered-street reference in it is a modern address. No street number in this report needs 1909 renumbering conversion: the district had almost no buildings before 1905 and its numbering was set with the names. Addresses that appear in the report solely as somebody's home are not recorded here, per the privacy limits in the root AGENTS.md — that covers four Parkside District Improvement Club officers' houses. Where such a house is also on the 1908 cottage list or carries a dated fact about the building itself, the building fact is recorded and the resident is not. Builders, architects, contractors and the merchant whose name the Williams Store carries are named in their building role, which the same rule permits.

findings.description: The Trocadero Inn, a two-storey wood-frame roadhouse with a steep dormered roof, stick ornament on the porch and a stone fireplace inside, built in 1892 by George M. Greene. It is the only structure in the Parkside known to predate 1905. Leased out as a resort with a deer park, boating pavilion and beer garden, it was where the political boss Abe Ruef was arrested in hiding in 1907 as the graft trials opened. It closed in 1916 and stands in Sigmund Stern Grove, bought by Rosalie Meyer Stern in 1931 and given to the city.

findings.description: Pinehurst Lodge, built in 1928 for the San Francisco Junior League as a home for children awaiting foster placements, to a design by Ashley, Evers and Hayes with J. S. Sampson Company as general contractors. Two storeys of brick under a hipped tile roof, Mediterranean in manner, its three wings enclosing a courtyard on the west, set on a large landscaped lot among modest row houses. Animal, ship and castle tiles line the recreation room; the visitors' room fireplace carries an Old King Cole frieze; the salon ceiling is inscribed in Latin from 1 Corinthians 13. It took a city-clubhouses award at the 1929 Northern California Architectural Exhibition at the de Young Museum, and has been owned by the Salvation Army since 1946.

findings.description: Abraham Lincoln High School, built in 1940 after years of lobbying by Parkside residents and a 1938 bond measure, to a design by Fred H. Meyer, Martin Rist and Timothy L. Pflueger.
